newsitem.title: UK: London funds face tough call on US after Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: London funds face tough call on US after Greenspan.

text.p: A surge in U.S. markets on benign testimony from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan is prompting London-based fund managers to re-evaluate their underweight positions in U.S. equities.
"There are battles breaking out in asset allocation committees all over Europe," said David Currie, a portfolio manager at Edinburgh Fund Managers who controls a U.S. equity book of $450 million.
"People are reconsidering if they really should be this underweight in the biggest market in the world."

Wall Street took Greenspan's comments on Tuesday that demand growth appears to have moderated as a green light to bid up shares to record levels, with Dow Jones industrials jumping 155 points to finish at 8,061.
But British and European fund managers have largely been underweight on the U.S. during the past two years and have missed out on much of its spectacular gain.

British fund managers are allocating about 27 percent of their global equity portfolios to the U.S. and Canada, according to a recent Reuters poll, as opposed to a benchmark figure of about 39 percent.
"It is a massive gamble that is not paying off and it is really, really hurting. It is hard to compensate for that elsewhere," Currie said.
Edinburgh Fund Managers has been moving its U.S. allocation towards the benchmark in recent months but is still underweight, Currie said.
"I'm agonising -- do I sit down at the asset allocation meeting and say now is the time to buy? It takes guts to say this market is up 27 percent this year and I'm going to buy it."
Fund managers generally agreed that Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkings testimony painted a picture of an economy benefiting from improved efficiencies and with no immediate threat from inflation.
But there was little consensus on what strategy that suggested, other than to carry very little cash in portfolios.

The economy Greenspan describes "is particularly positive for the investing environment, if you believe it is sustainable," said Andrew McMenigall, who manages 200 million sterling in U.S. equities for Ivory & Sime.
"But the longer people believe that (scenario) the more risky it becomes when any element of the argument unwinds."
To guard against damage from a correction, he is trying to be better diversified from a sector standpoint, and is moving his holdings to be more in line with the broader S&P 500.
Chris Galleymore of Henderson Investors, who manages more than $1 billion in the U.S., is considering a shift into cyclical stocks and away from growth shares.

"If what Greenspan is saying is that we can maintain high levels of growth for at least another couple of years without inflation picking up, then we may have to switch to more of the cyclical stocks, where we have been anticipating profit margin pressure showing up."
But he added that if pressure is going to be delayed, on a tactical basis Henderson would consider moving away from growth companies.
"We have to look at what he is saying about the shape of the economy over the next two years and ask ourselves do we want to rotate. That's the really difficult decision," Galleymore said.
He has also been raising his cash allocation, but only to about the five percent level.
For now, fund managers will be keeping a wary eye on inflation and earnings.
"If you are looking at valuations, this market is at 19 or 20 times and that is the highest it has ever been at this late point in the cycle," said Currie.
"But I think people see the U.S. market and the U.S. economy as being tremendously strong. You can pick holes and say it's looking overvalued at the moment, but there is tremendous momentum."
